'''''Asplenium australasicum''''', the '''bird's nest fern''' or '''crow's nest fern''', is an epiphytic Australasian species of [[fern]] in the family [[Aspleniaceae]].<ref name="mediterran">{{cite book|last=Elliot|first=Rodger |title=Australian Plants for Mediterranean Climate Gardens|publisher=Rosenberg Publishing|year=2003|pages=45|isbn=1-877058-18-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TJi4uzF31UQC&dq=Asplenium+australasicum&pg=PA45}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Asplenium australasicum'' was originally described by English botanist John Smith in 1857 as ''Neottopteris australasica''.<ref>{{APNI | name =''Neottopteris australasica''  J.Sm. | id = 25991}}</ref> He had reclassified the already known ''[[Asplenium nidus|A. nidus]]'' in its own genus ''Neottopteris''. Other botanists reclassified the genus as a section, ''Thamnopteris'', within the genus ''[[Asplenium]]'',<ref name="murakami">{{cite journal|author=Noriaki Murakami|author2=Mikio Watanabe|author3=Jun Yokoyama|author4=Yoko Yatabe|author5=Hisako Iwasaki|author6=Shunsuke Serizawa|name-list-style=amp|year=1999|title=Molecular Taxonomic Study and Revision of the Three Japanese Species of ''Asplenium'' sect. ''Thamnopteris''|journal=[[Journal of Plant Research]]|volume=112|issue=1|pages=15–25|doi=10.1007/PL00013856|s2cid=23985191}}</ref> and [[William Jackson Hooker]] gave it its current binomial name in 1859.<ref>{{APNI | name =''Asplenium australasicum'' (J.Sm.) Hook. | id = 51413}}</ref> Although the section ''Thamnopteris'' is distinctive, defining the species has been difficult as the morphology of the plants is so simple.<ref name="murakami"/> ''A. australasicum'' has been confused with (and called) ''A. nidus'',<ref name=Fairley>{{cite book |author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |page=41|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}}</ref> and Japanese populations which were considered to be ''A. australasicum'' by their morphology have been found to be genetically distinct and reclassified as a new species, ''[[Asplenium setori|A. setoi]]''.<ref name="murakami"/>

A global phylogeny of ''Asplenium'' published in 2020 divided the genus into eleven clades,{{sfn|Xu|Zhang|Rothfels|Smith|2020|p=27}} which were given informal names pending further taxonomic study. ''A. australasicum'' belongs to the "''Neottopteris'' clade",{{sfn|Xu|Zhang|Rothfels|Smith|2020|p=31}} members of which generally have somewhat leathery leaf tissue. While the subclades of this group are poorly resolved, several of them share a characteristic "bird's-nest fern" morphology with entire leaves and fused veins near the margin.{{sfn|Xu|Zhang|Rothfels|Smith|2020|p=41}} Both the 2020 study{{sfn|Xu|Zhang|Rothfels|Smith|2020|p=41}} and a 2015 molecular study found that ''A. australasicum'' is polyphyletic, meaning that some populations were not closely related to others—''A. australasicum'' from Fiji and Vanauatu were not closely related to ''A. australasicum'' from Australia and New Caledonia. Hence a revision with sampling of the species across its range was required to delineate the taxon and identify cryptic species.<ref name=Ohlsen2015>{{cite journal|vauthors=Ohlsen DJ, Perrie LR, Shepherd LD, Brownsey PJ, Bayly MJ |date=2015|title=Phylogeny of the fern family Aspleniaceae in Australasia and the southwestern Pacific|journal=[[Australian Systematic Botany]]|volume=27|issue=6|pages=355–71 | doi=10.1071/sb14043|doi-access=free}}</ref> ''A. australasicum'' forms a clade with the morphologically similar ''[[Asplenium nidus|A. nidus]]'' ''[[sensu lato]]'', but other bird's-nest ferns such as ''[[Asplenium antiquum|A. antiquum]]'' and ''[[Asplenium phyllitidis|A. phyllitidis]]'' form a separate subclade which is not particularly closely related.{{sfn|Xu|Zhang|Rothfels|Smith|2020|p=31}}

==Description==
''Asplenium australasicum'' grows as shrubby plant, with a rosette of yellow-green fronds which are 60 to 80 cm (24–32 in) long and 3 to 21 cm (1.2–8.4 in) wide.<ref name="floransw">{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Asplenium |species=australasicum|author= Peter G. Wilson}}</ref> It can be distinguished from ''A. nidus'' by its prominent midrib under its fronds, giving the fronds a keeled appearance.<ref name="murakami"/> The spores form in parallel lines which run in parallel with the veins and oblique to the midrib.<ref name=Fairley/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''A. australasicum'' grows on rocks or as an [[epiphyte]] on trees and is native to eastern New South Wales and Queensland.<ref name="floransw"/> The clumps can reach a large size, with the centre of the fern acting as a reservoir for debris.<ref name=Fairley/> The colonial botanist [[William Woolls]] wrote "... as a caution to fern gatherers, sometimes a species of [[Red-bellied black snake|black snake]] coils itself up in the centre" (of the birds nest fern).<ref>Les Robinson – Field Guide to the Native Plants of Sydney, {{ISBN|978-0-7318-1211-0}} page 306</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Asplenium australasicum'' specimens were taken from logged areas, which helped them become popular in horticulture.<ref name=Fairley/> It adapts readily to cultivation, as long as it has good drainage. Poor drainage renders it vulnerable to rotting.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://anpsa.org.au/a-aust.html|title=Asplenium australasicum|author=Walters, Brian|date=November 2007|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia)|accessdate=10 November 2011}}</ref> It can be grown in a tub or barrel.<ref name="mediterran"/> In cultivation it is occasionally attacked by white [[coconut scale]] on the underside of the fronds.<ref name="mediterran"/>

==Uses==
Apart from its use as an ornamental plant, bird's nest fern is also a popular vegetable in Taiwan, particularly in the Eastern part of the island, where the young emerging fronds of both ''A. australasicum'' and [[Asplenium nidus|''A. nidus'']] are used as a leafy vegetable, from either wild or cultivated plants.<ref>{{cite web|last=Anonymous |title=Bird's nest fern (Vegetable uses) |url=http://libnts.avrdc.org.tw/fulltext_pdf/ebook1/10-7%20birds%20nest%20fern.pdf |publisher=AVRDC, The World Vegetable Center |accessdate=27 November 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426004956/http://libnts.avrdc.org.tw/fulltext_pdf/ebook1/10-7%20birds%20nest%20fern.pdf |archivedate=26 April 2012 }}</ref>
